title: The hardest gift
hookLine: the traditions speak of forgiveness, and none of them pretends it's easy
carry: sending a guard away from his post

cards: Some names land like a small stone in the chest. A parent. An old friend.
A business partner. An ex. Years go by, the stone is still there, and somebody says, kindly, just let it go.
How, exactly? That question opens the next stretch of this path. For the coming weeks you'll hear what the traditions say about forgiveness: Jewish voices first, then others, one at a time.
And before any of them speaks, one thing worth saying plainly: the texts ahead don't pretend it's easy.

teach.b: First, why call it a gift. Forgiving gives something away: the right to get even, the story where you're owed. Nobody can force it out of you.
That's what makes it a gift, and what makes it hard. Second, two old voices.
The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in one line: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love", and calls this an old rule.

The Qur'an, in a verse about answering a wrong, allows a response in kind, then says that whoever pardons and makes peace, their reward is with God. Neither pretends the hurt didn't happen. Both point past it.
Some teachers today, from more than one tradition, draw a line between forgiving and excusing. Forgiving doesn't say it was fine, or mean pretending to forget.
For some, it doesn't mean walking back into the same room with the same person.

The traditions draw these lines in different places: whether the one who did wrong has to ask first, who is able to forgive what, and whether forgiving means making up. Fourth, why it's hard. Anger is often doing a job.
It guards a wound. It keeps a record, so the thing won't happen again.
Asking it to stand down can feel like sending a guard away from his post. That's why, on this path, forgiveness is a practice, not a switch. It might take one try.
It might take a great many.

how: Forgiveness is taught across the traditions: in Jewish practice around the Days of Awe, in Christian prayer, in Islamic teaching on pardon, and in Buddhist practices of loving-kindness, each with its own understanding of who forgives and how.

o: waiting until the other person has paid back in full
giving up the claim to get even, freely and often slowly

games.q: someone hurt you, and the anger is still there. by the Dhammapada's old rule, what ends hatred?
games.why: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love." the Dhammapada calls it an old rule.

practice: Let one name come up, someone you haven't forgiven, not the biggest one, and notice what happens in the jaw, the chest, the hands.
You don't have to forgive them now; just say the name quietly and let it sit beside you, like someone in the next seat of a bus. If you pray, you can bring that name into your prayer, just as it is.
